record.paper_title: Invitation to H-systems in higher dimensions: known results, new facts, and related open problems
record.context_brief: Endpoint commutator spaces for H-system data
record.original_question: Fix H bounded and Lipschitz on R^{n+1}, let u be in W^{1,n}(R^n,R^{n+1}), and set b=H(u), so that b is in W^{1,n}(R^n) intersect L^infty(R^n). Determine the largest subspace V of the Hardy space H^1(R^n) such that the commutator [b,I] maps V to L^{n/(n-1)}(R^n), or to W^{1,1}(R^n) in the variant question; determine whether V contains the n by n minors of Du; determine the largest subspace V such that all commutators [b,R_alpha] with the Riesz transforms map V to L^1(R^n); determine whether du^1 wedge ... wedge du^n has an atomic decomposition into b-atoms, meaning standard atoms additionally orthogonal to b; and determine whether the answers change when u is also assumed to solve an H-system.

evidence.quote: Problem 4.1. Fix H bounded and Lipschitz on Rn+1 , and u ∈ W 1,n (Rn , Rn+1 ), so that b = H(u) ∈ W 1,n (Rn ) ∩ L∞ (Rn ).
What is the largest subspace V ⊂ H1 (Rn ) such that [b, I] : V → Ln/(n−1) (Rn )? What is the answer if we replace Ln/(n−1) (Rn ) by W 1,1 (Rn )? Does this V contain the n × n minors of Du?
What is the largest subspace V ⊂ H1 (Rn ) such that all commutators [b, Rα ] of the multiplication by b with the Riesz transforms Rα , α = 1, . . . , n, map V → L1 (Rn )?
Does du1 ∧ . . . ∧ dun have an atomic decomposition into b-atoms, i.e. standard atoms that are, in addition, orthogonal to b?
Do the answers to the above questions change if u is not just an element of W 1,n , but also a solution to an H-system?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let n ≥ 2. Fix a bounded Lipschitz function H : R^{n+1} → R, and let u ∈ W^{1,n}(R^n, R^{n+1}). Set b := H ∘ u, so that b ∈ W^{1,n}(R^n) ∩ L^∞(R^n). Let H^1(R^n) denote the real Hardy space, let R_α (α = 1, …, n) denote the Riesz transforms on R^n, and let I denote the Riesz potential of order 1 (so that ∇I is essentially the vector of Riesz transforms). For a function b ∈ L^∞, the commutator [b, T] is the operator f ↦ bT(f) − T(bf). A standard H^1-atom a supported in a ball B is said to be a b-atom if, in addition, ∫_B a(x) b(x) dx = 0.

Address the following questions.

(a) Determine the largest linear subspace V ⊂ H^1(R^n) such that the commutator [b, I] maps V continuously into L^{n/(n−1)}(R^n). 

(b) Determine the largest linear subspace V ⊂ H^1(R^n) such that [b, I] maps V continuously into the Sobolev space W^{1,1}(R^n).

(c) In (a) and (b), determine whether V contains all n × n minors of the Jacobian matrix Du (viewed as elements of H^1(R^n)).

(d) Determine the largest linear subspace V ⊂ H^1(R^n) such that, for every α = 1, …, n, the commutator [b, R_α] maps V continuously into L^1(R^n).

(e) Determine whether the n-form du^1 ∧ ⋯ ∧ du^n (equivalently, the Jacobian of u, suitably interpreted as a distribution in H^1) admits an atomic decomposition into b-atoms.

(f) Determine whether the answers to (a)–(e) change under the additional assumption that u solves an H-system, i.e. Δu = 2H(u) u_{x_1} ∧ ⋯ ∧ u_{x_n} (in the appropriate weak sense).
artifact.status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open problem in a survey on H-systems in higher dimensions. A web search did not locate any subsequent work resolving the specific questions about the largest subspace V ⊂ H^1(R^n) for which [b, I] and [b, R_α] satisfy the stated endpoint mapping properties when b = H(u), nor about b-atomic decompositions of du^1 ∧ ⋯ ∧ du^n. Related work on commutators, Jacobians, and Hardy spaces exists, but no resolution of this precise problem was found.
